Les rénovictions qui sévissent dans les: Renovictions are plaguing Montréal's working-class neighbourhoods and touch on a number of complex issues. When traditional remedies fail the most marginalized tenants, what solutions take their reality into account?
Voici ce que proposent des citoyens enga: Here is what engaged citizens and boroughs are proposing to try to overcome these obstacles.
Veronica Mockler, une artiste engagée, c: Veronica Mockler, an activist artist, believes art can be an effective way to fight renovictions. In the spring of 2019, in collaboration with artist Sofia Blondin and eight tenants from Côte-des-Neiges, she presented <l1>L’ADRESSE</l1>, an art performance that shed light on these tenants' experiences. The tenants who took part in the performance spoke about their experiences in housing in the neighbourhood. With L’ADRESSE, the artists wanted to focus on Côte-des-Neiges. “It's a neighbourhood that is seen as a stepping stone for newcomers who are starting their stay in Montréal,” explains Ms. Mockler.
Un long processus créatif s’ensuivit pou: A long creative process followed for the artists, who, at the request of specialized researchers, including Dr. Karoline Truchon of the Amplifier group, wanted to make the problem easier to understand and educate citizens about the housing crisis affecting Côte-des-Neiges. Ms. Blondin and Ms. Mockler conducted more than 30 interviews with people who live or work in the neighbourhood.
Elles ont discuté avec des locataires, d: They spoke with tenants, landlords, City officials, inspectors, community organizations and activist groups. It was important to them to listen closely to what people had to say. “People don't necessarily know their rights. They need housing quickly for their whole family. So tenants take what they're offered, and there are landlords who profit from that situation,” says the artist. These testimonies were shocking for the artists to hear. Having only recently arrived, many tenants are not familiar with the ins and outs of renting housing in the city.
« Deux participants ont vécu dans des ma: “Two participants lived in rooming houses and thought that was the norm for housing in Quebec and Canada,” explains Ms. Mockler. “There's a truly systemic problem that allows private landlords to exploit people over what is a fundamental right.”
Avec L’ADRESSE, les artistes ont voulu a: With L’ADRESSE, the artists wanted to go much further than what engaged artists usually do. Instead of simply consulting tenants and drawing on their stories to make a work of art, it was the tenants themselves who led the artistic project. By giving them a platform to share their stories, the creators hoped to spark political change. They also wanted to create an educational space that would let residents in the audience learn about their rights. In producing such a performance, the two artists also made sure their work would not be behind the walls of a museum or theatre, places that are often inaccessible to people in working-class neighbourhoods, but right in the heart of the Côte-des-Neiges community.
L’ADRESSE a été présentée dans le secteu: L’ADRESSE was presented in the Triangle sector, a former working-class area undergoing rapid gentrification, located close to the former racetrack, where many housing struggles have taken place. “We invited politicians, including the mayor of Côte-des-Neiges–Notre-Dame-de-Grâce,” says Ms. Mockler. Art was used as a pretext to draw them in and put them face to face with the issue. For Ms. Mockler, this is a major victory: the residents who took part in the project were able to be heard by decision-makers. The activist artist remembers one resident in particular, Mr. Ismael. A refugee from Burkina Faso, he had arrived in Canada only a few months before the performance. After his performance, he was able to sit down with Sue Montgomery, the borough mayor, and discuss his situation.
« La mairesse lui a demandé ses coordonn: “The mayor asked him for his contact information, saying that rooming houses are illegal. She had the house where he was living shut down,” Ms. Mockler exclaims proudly. “There's a real effect, and not only for people who appreciate art. It brought about real change in society. That was my goal!” Line Bonneau, a volunteer with Projet Genèse, a community organization focused on social justice in Côte-des-Neiges, was deeply moved by her participation in L’ADRESSE. Ms. Bonneau, who has not always been a tenant, sold her house before leaving the country for a few years. When she came back to Montréal, she decided to get involved with Projet Genèse. One of her tasks was going door to door to inform tenants of their rights.
« C’est là que j’ai découvert qu’à moins: “That's when I discovered that less than a kilometre away, there were incredible stories of abuse. When you're a homeowner, you're not aware of this kind of thing,” says the volunteer. In her view, the balance of power is so heavily in landlords' favour that they rarely face consequences. Her performance in L’ADRESSE deals with this grim reality, which she has witnessed over the past nine years. Ms. Bonneau believes that projects like this one, which involve citizens, are an effective way to fight the scourge.
« Je crois que ce format théâtral peut p: “I believe this theatrical format can push people to become more aware,” she sums up. For Anna-Maria Camino, another participant in the piece, the experience was very enriching. During our interview, she strikes a pose, flexing her biceps. It's how she ended her performance in L’ADRESSE. “I stood like a warrior. I was wearing makeup and a wig, it was great. Afterwards, lots of people congratulated me,” she says proudly. Her partner, her colleagues, her mother, her stepfather and her sister attended her performance. Her sister's presence meant a lot to Ms. Camino. “She's very busy, with her kids and her job, so she rarely has time to come and support my projects. It's the first time since we came to Canada that she's had the chance to do it,” smiles the Côte-des-Neiges resident.
À la suite de la représentation de L’ADR: Following the performance of L’ADRESSE, which she attended, Sue Montgomery, mayor of Côte-des-Neiges–Notre-Dame-de-Grâce, introduced new by-laws. “We banned renovations that are apartment expansions,” she says. Her team has also hired inspectors and set up a program that tackles unsanitary housing. If work deemed necessary is not carried out by the landlord, it is then undertaken by the borough, and the bill is sent to the landlord. Ms. Montgomery also says she has increased the amount of the fine given to landlords who do not make the necessary repairs.
Toutefois, ce changement n’apparaît pas: However, this change does not appear in the Urban Planning By-law of the Côte-des-Neiges–Notre-Dame-de-Grâce borough. A new measure has been put in place to help deal with rising housing prices. “It targets Airbnb, which takes apartments off the rental market and drives up the prices of the apartments that are still available,” says Ms. Montgomery. This type of rental is now permitted only in private homes.
Pour les femmes, les problèmes ne se lim: For women, the problems are not limited to access to decent housing. It is not uncommon for a mother to be refused a rental on the pretext that she has young children. Landlords also take advantage of these women's precarious position.
« Des hommes qui sont propriétaires vont: “Men who are landlords will knock on single mothers' doors at any hour of the night,” says Ms. Mockler. “It's truly an intersectional problem.
Ces citoyennes sont vulnérables parce qu: These women are vulnerable because they've just arrived in the country, they have no status, job or financial means, and they are targeted because of their gender.” Sue Montgomery, mayor of Côte-des-Neiges–Notre-Dame-de-Grâce, encourages victims to call her office in full confidentiality to get support. She also says she is open to working with the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal in this regard.
Les limites des comités logement, Margot: Margot Silvestro knows the limits of housing committees well. The community organizer with the Comité d’action des citoyens de Verdun (CACV) is caught off guard when people who speak neither French nor English face renovictions. “It's a challenge, especially when they're newcomers. They may have additional fears linked to their immigration status, not know the rules well, or not want to cause trouble,” explains Ms. Silvestro. The organization cannot rely on a network of translators, and the responsibility for finding one often falls on the citizen in distress. Ms. Camino is a support worker at Femmes du monde, an organization that aims to bring together women in Côte-des-Neiges.
Elle milite pour le logement dans le qua: She campaigns for housing in the neighbourhood where she has lived for 15 years. Her activism is driven by her own housing difficulties and the heartfelt values her Argentinian parents passed on to her. “I was renting an apartment on Équerre Street, and the heat was never turned on. The landlord was very controlling. When I complained, they gave me a space heater to shut me up,” says Ms. Camino, who had to bundle up in blankets to stay warm. The support worker considers herself lucky to speak French and to have been able to voice her discontent about this situation. Many of the people she helps don't have that luck. They see in her a glimmer of hope. “When complainants hear me speak Spanish, they let it all out.
Ils me disent qu’ils évitent de se plain: They tell me they avoid complaining to their landlord for fear of being kicked out,” she explains. “I tell them they don't have to resign themselves to their fate, and that there are rights here that can protect them. They don't have to live with terror, with fear – and with pests in their apartment.” The activist believes one solution is to have frontline workers who speak different languages. She observes that it puts people at ease. She has appeared at the Administrative Housing Tribunal (TAL) as an interpreter on several occasions.
Claudia Leduc, artiste et militante, est: Claudia Leduc, an artist and activist, is an administrator of several Facebook groups of tenants in solidarity, united against gentrification. These groups are a way to spread information about housing law from one tenant to another. On their page, you regularly see posts from tenants going through legal proceedings, people sharing articles on the latest housing news in Montréal, and citizens giving advice on renting in the city.
« J’invite les gens à se joindre aux gro: “I invite people to join citizen mutual-aid groups, for example the Facebook group Locataires unis contre la gentrification, to talk about their problems and learn about their rights,” encourages Ms. Leduc. She also runs a private group for those who want to discuss their situation in more detail. With these groups, she hopes to make help and information about housing rights more accessible. She also encourages citizens to enter the price of their rent in the <l1>public citizen rent registry,</l1> which lets people looking for housing see the previous rents for an address. In the same spirit, she advises every tenant to leave a copy of their lease for the new tenant when moving out.
Mme Leduc rappelle que, pour faire des t: Ms. Leduc points out that written notice is required to carry out work or proceed with an eviction.
« La plupart du temps, lorsque les propr: “Most of the time, when landlords make verbal threats, they're not ready to go through the steps of sending notices. They want the person to leave of their own accord,” she explains. If they know the financial situation of the tenant they're trying to evict, they may try to convince them to leave by offering them a sum of money. The activist strongly recommends that tenants keep written records of all their interactions with their landlord.
Leslie Touré Kapo, chercheur en sécurité: Leslie Touré Kapo, a researcher in urban security, believes Montréal can draw inspiration from other cities around the world when it comes to renovictions. “In Paris, they've just put in place a rent cap. We could also set up a vacant-housing tax system, as in Barcelona,” suggests Mr. Kapo. The specialist believes we need to look at what certain cities are doing to protect access to housing in order to better understand how to meet the needs of people in working-class neighbourhoods.
Selon le chercheur, les candidats à l’él: According to the researcher, candidates in Montréal's municipal election can do much more on the issue of housing. He wants to see them put forward a concrete plan. “Access to affordable, decent housing that meets public health standards, access to housing close to public facilities and infrastructure, such as public transit, roads and lighting – these are the questions candidates should be asking themselves. We need to think about urban space in all its complexity, not just housing,” he says. Mr. Kapo also believes candidates should ask themselves about language barriers and access to justice for tenants facing renovictions.
« Si, par exemple, une famille monoparen: “If, for example, a single-parent family with precarious work has problems with their landlord, how can they take action?” he wonders. In Villeray–Saint-Michel–Parc-Extension, Mayor Giuliana Fumagalli says she is working very hard on the issue of renovictions. “As a borough, we have the power to put in place measures to try to limit evictions for repossession that are carried out in bad faith,” the mayor points out. Building permits also fall under its jurisdiction.
« Je souhaite que les permis soient émis: “I want permits to be issued only upon presentation of a document proving that tenants have been informed of their rights and that an agreement has been reached,” she says. She is also asking that administrative services inform tenants of their rights and direct them to tenant rights organizations in their borough. Ms. Fumagalli intends to support these organizations financially to help them spread information in several languages. She has also worked with the borough's three housing committees to develop a form that tenants can use to protect themselves.
Le document, qui est illustré de pictogr: The document, which is illustrated with pictograms meant to make it more accessible, also contains a map showing where the neighbourhood's unsanitary housing is located. It also includes a formal notice procedure directed at landlords e
Si vous souhaitez faire inspecter un log: If you want to have a dwelling inspected in the Côte-des-Neiges–Notre-Dame-de-Grâce borough, you can contact the mayor's office or go to the borough's access office, at 5160 Décarie Boulevard, Suite 600.
Pour obtenir le formulaire destiné aux l: To get the form intended for Parc-Extension tenants, just dial 311 and go to a borough committee or to the borough's access office, at 405 Ogilvy Street.
